title: First exchange
verifiedBy: Claude Fable 5 — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: French makes a choice English does not: vous for anyone you are not close to, and for more than one person; tu for family and close friends. This course writes vous throughout, so vous êtes is the second person you learn — and bonjour, not the friendly salut, is its greeting.
A yes/no question is the statement, unchanged, said with a rising voice and written with a question mark: Vous êtes anglais ? beside Vous êtes anglais. Nothing moves and nothing is added.

English builds a question out of "do", or by hauling "are" to the front. French has no word standing in for "do" at all, and moving the verb (Êtes-vous anglais ?) is a formal written register this course does not use. Reaching for either is the English habit, not a French option.

A question word never drags the verb with it. It can stand in front — Comment ça va ? — or stay where the answer would go — Vous vous appelez comment ? Either way the rest of the sentence keeps the order it had.
ça va has no word for "you" inside it — literally "it goes" — so it is the question and the answer both, and it is safe with anyone whatever the register.

An adjective agrees with the SUBJECT — whoever or whatever the sentence is about, not whoever is speaking: Je suis fatigué (a man about himself) · Vous êtes fatiguée ? (asked of a woman). Here the -e is silent, so the two spellings are one sound: the ear cannot check what the eye must.
Oui and Non are one-word answers, exactly as in English, and the sentence behind them is the plain statement with nothing removed.
French puts a space in front of ? and !, so the mark stands a little clear of the last word: Ça va ? The mark is the only thing a question adds in writing.

words.note: One greeting for the whole day until the evening, safe with anyone. salut is the friendly one and belongs with tu, the register this course does not write.

sentences.trap: English picks a greeting by the clock — good morning, good afternoon, good evening. French does not: bonjour covers all of it, and there is no separate "good morning" to translate.
sentences.sound: bohn-ZHOOR. The on is nasal — the air goes through the nose and the n itself is never sounded — and the j is the soft sound in the middle of "measure".

variations.changed: swap the name — bonjour itself never changes
the greeting carries straight on into the question
greeting first, then M1's introduction — two sentences in one breath

mistake.why: There is no French "good morning": bonjour covers the day until evening. Bon matin is the English shape translated word for word — Quebec says it, France does not.

sentences.usage: The opening of any exchange, with anyone at all.
sentences.mnemonic: bon + jour — a good day, whatever hour of it you are in.

words.note: Literally "it goes". There is no word for "you" in it, which is why it works as question and answer and costs the tu/vous choice nothing. A rising voice makes it the question; a flat one the answer.

sentences.trap: "How are you?" does not survive being translated word for word. Comment êtes-vous ? is real French and asks what sort of person you are, not how you are doing. The wellbeing question is ça va ? or comment ça va ?
sentences.sound: sa VA — the ç is a plain s, never a k, and both a's are open. The question is carried entirely by the voice rising at the end.

variations.changed: drop the greeting — the question stands on its own
a question word in front makes the fuller version; nothing else moves
the same two words as the answer — only the voice stops rising

mistake.why: That asks what sort of person you are, not how you are doing. Wellbeing runs on ça va — Bonjour, ça va ?

sentences.usage: The second line of almost every exchange, said to anyone.
sentences.mnemonic: "It goes?" — French asks how things are going, not how you are.

words.note: well — the word that goes with a verb. Its neighbour bon means "good" and goes with a noun, so ça va bien is right and ça va bon is not: English blurs the two and French does not.
thank you — one word for both of English's, and it needs no "you" after it.

sentences.trap: English answers "How are you?" with a word about itself — "I'm fine". French answers about how things are going: ça va bien. There is no I in the answer at all.
sentences.sound: bien is one syllable, byan, with the vowel nasal and the n never sounded. merci is mair-SEE, the stress falling on the last syllable as it does on almost every French word.

variations.changed: drop bien — ça va alone is already the answer
the thanks first — the two halves are independent

variations.display: Ça va bien, et je suis fatigué
variations.changed: a second clause behind the answer, with the speaker back in it

mistake.why: bon is the adjective "good" and goes with a noun; bien is the adverb "well" and goes with a verb. va is a verb, so it takes bien.

sentences.mnemonic: A verb keeps company with bien; a noun keeps company with bon.

words.note: how. Bolting it on moves nothing else: Comment ça va ? is Ça va ? with comment in front. In speech it can also stay where the answer would go — Vous vous appelez comment ? The final -t is silent.

sentences.trap: English moves the verb after "how" — "how ARE you". French leaves the sentence exactly as it was and puts the question word where it likes: in front, or where the answer would go.
sentences.sound: ko-MAHN — the ent is nasal and the final -t is silent, so nothing sounds at the end at all.

variations.changed: drop the question word — the short form asks the same thing
the name comes after, marked off by a comma
the same question word on M1's naming verb — this time left where the answer would go, and still nothing inverted

mistake.why: comment with être asks what someone is LIKE, not how they are doing. Wellbeing runs on ça va: Comment ça va ?

sentences.usage: A slightly fuller "how are you" — a shade more attentive than ça va ? on its own.
sentences.mnemonic: Put comment in front and change nothing else.

words.note: tired. It agrees with the subject: fatigué for a man, fatiguée for a woman — and here the extra -e is genuinely silent, the one agreement the ear cannot check. fatigue without the accent is a noun.

sentences.trap: English tiredness is a fact about you and nothing on the word shows it. French writes who you are into the word itself, and gets no help from the sound while doing it.
sentences.sound: fa-tee-GAY. The gu is a hard g, never a j sound, and the final é is the clean "ay" the accent marks.

variations.changed: the -e for a woman — written, and not heard at all
est for a third person, and the ending follows Anne
êtes for the person spoken to, and a rising voice makes it a question

mistake.why: The accent is a letter. fatigue without it is the noun "tiredness", so this says "I am tiredness". Write fatigué.

sentences.usage: How you are, when ça va bien would not be true.
sentences.mnemonic: The accent is what turns the tiredness into the tired person.

sentences.glossEn: lit. "You are tired?" — asked of a woman

words.note: you. vous is for anyone you are not close to, and for more than one person; tu is for family and close friends. This course writes vous everywhere, because vous is never rude. It always takes êtes.

sentences.trap: English has one "you" and never has to decide. French decides every time you open your mouth, and the safe answer with someone you have just met is always vous.
sentences.sound: voo-ZET. The -s of vous is silent on its own, but in front of a vowel it wakes up as a z and links straight into êtes — that link is what makes the pair sound like one word.

variations.changed: asked of a man — the -e goes, and nothing changes in the sound
the same words as a statement — only the mark and the voice change
swap the adjective for a job — and after être the job still stands bare

mistake.why: vous takes êtes, always. est belongs to il and elle, never to the person you are speaking to.

sentences.usage: Asking after someone you are not close to — which, in this course, is everyone.
sentences.mnemonic: vous êtes travel together: voo-ZET, one sound, one pair.

words.note: English, the adjective — anglais for a man, anglaise for a woman, and the -e wakes the silent final -s into a z. Lowercase, like français: only the noun for the person, un Anglais, takes a capital.

sentences.trap: English asks by moving the verb — "ARE you English?". French asks by leaving everything exactly where it is and letting the voice rise. Êtes-vous anglais ? exists, needs its hyphen, and belongs to formal writing.
sentences.sound: ahn-GLEH, with the an nasal and the final -s silent. vous êtes still links: voo-ZET ahn-GLEH.

variations.changed: asked of a woman — and the -e turns the final -s into a z
swap the nationality — the question shape is untouched
a statement about someone else — est, and no question mark

mistake.why: Inversion needs its hyphen — Êtes-vous anglais ? — and it is the formal written question. The everyday one is the plain statement with a rising voice: Vous êtes anglais ?

sentences.usage: A yes/no question, asked of anyone.
sentences.mnemonic: Move nothing. Let the voice do the asking.

words.note: yes. It answers on its own, and the full sentence behind it is the plain statement with nothing taken out.

sentences.trap: English can answer with a shrunken echo — "Yes, I am". French does not echo: it either says oui alone, or says the whole sentence.
sentences.sound: wee — two letters, one sound, and nothing at all like the English "oui" people say as a joke.

variations.changed: the answer on its own — the sentence behind it is optional

variations.cue: Yes, I am English (a woman speaking)
variations.changed: the -e because of who is speaking about herself
swap what is being confirmed — M1's origin frame behind the same oui

mistake.why: No un after être in front of a nationality: je suis anglais. The capitalised noun un Anglais is a person, not a description.

sentences.mnemonic: oui, then the whole sentence or nothing.

words.note: no. Like oui it answers on its own, and the sentence behind it is a plain positive statement — the two-word negation ne … pas is a separate machine, and it arrives in L1-M3.

sentences.trap: Answering non does not make the sentence behind it negative. Non, je suis français is a No followed by something perfectly positive: the correction, not the denial.
sentences.sound: The on is nasal and the n is never sounded — nohn, with the sound finishing in the nose rather than on the tongue.

variations.changed: the answer alone, with no sentence behind it
a job instead of a nationality behind the same non
the correction is about someone else — est, and the feminine ending

mistake.why: non answers the question; the sentence behind it still needs its verb. Non, je suis français.

sentences.mnemonic: non is the answer; the sentence after it is untouched.

words.note: goodbye — two words always written apart and said together. au is à welded onto le, and revoir is "to see again": "until the seeing again". The closing that matches bonjour, safe with anyone.

sentences.trap: English closes with a word about going — "goodbye", "see you". French closes with a word about the next meeting, and it is fixed: nothing inside au revoir can be swapped.
sentences.sound: oh ruh-VWAR. The r's are made at the back of the throat, and the -oir ending is a wa sound with the r after it.

variations.changed: swap the name — au revoir itself never changes
no name at all — the closing stands alone
the thanks first, then the closing — the ordinary end of a counter exchange

mistake.why: à and le are welded into au here, and the phrase is fixed: au revoir. À revoir is not French.

sentences.mnemonic: Not "goodbye" but "until we see each other again".
